Stage 3 · Grammar

How things were, and what people did

Two forms for the finished past — and only one of them works everywhere.

Read these four sentences.
  • He used to leave the house at ten past seven.
  • He would walk the same route every morning.
  • There used to be a company festival every summer.
  • My grandfather used to have the same desk for forty years.
In which two sentences could you not use would?
The past simple can describe a past habit. Used to adds that it has stopped.

I walked to school every day is perfectly correct English for a past routine. So why does the language need used to at all? Because the past simple says only that something happened; used to says that it happened regularly and that it does not happen now. That implied contrast between then and now is the entire communicative point of the structure.

Two forms share this territory, and they do not cover the same ground. Used to works for both repeated actions and past states: I used to work nights, There used to be a factory here, He used to have long hair. Would works only for repeated actions. You cannot say There would be a factory here or He would have long hair, because be and have describe states, not activities.

Would has a second limitation that is stylistic rather than grammatical: it normally needs the past time frame to be established already. Starting a story with I would walk to school sounds odd; When I was ten, I would walk to school is natural. This is why would feels at home in nostalgic storytelling and less so in a bare statement of fact.

One purely formal point causes more errors than anything else here. In the negative and the question, the d disappears: didn’t use to, Did you use to…? Writing didn’t used to is extremely common and is not accepted in careful English. And do not confuse this structure with be used to or get used to + -ing, which mean ‘be accustomed to’ and have nothing to do with past habits.

Before you look at the table: the table below shows which form covers actions, which covers states, and what happens to the spelling in negatives and questions. Check the states column first — that is where would stops working.
The two forms, side by side
 used towould

 RightWrong

Ask two questions. Is it a repeated action or a state? If it is a state, only used to works. Is it one single event? Then neither works — use the past simple.

Both mean it is over. I used to smoke tells the listener you do not smoke now. That is the whole point of the form; you never need to add “but not any more”.

The mistake to avoid. After did, the -d disappears: Did you use to…?, I didn’t use to… — exactly like every other verb after did.

Do not confuse it with be used to. I used to drive = I drove in the past. I’m used to driving = it feels normal to me now. Different meaning, different grammar.

Full grammar reference — used to and would — past habits and past states

What it is

Two ways of describing what was normal in the past but is not now. Used to + base verb covers both repeated actions and past states. Would + base verb covers repeated actions only, and needs a past time frame already established. Both carry the implication that the situation has changed.

What it means, and what it does

The past simple can describe a past habit perfectly well (I walked to school every day), but it does not say that things are different now. I used to walk to school does: it tells the listener the habit has ended. That contrast between then and now is the entire communicative point of the structure, and it is why the form belongs in a lesson about how working life has changed.

When and why we use it

I walked to school every day is perfectly correct English for a past routine. So why does the language need used to at all? Because the past simple says only that something happened; used to says that it happened regularly and that it does not happen now. That implied contrast between then and now is the entire communicative point of the structure.

Two forms share this territory, and they do not cover the same ground. Used to works for both repeated actions and past states: I used to work nights, There used to be a factory here, He used to have long hair. Would works only for repeated actions. You cannot say There would be a factory here or He would have long hair, because be and have describe states, not activities.

Would has a second limitation that is stylistic rather than grammatical: it normally needs the past time frame to be established already. Starting a story with I would walk to school sounds odd; When I was ten, I would walk to school is natural. This is why would feels at home in nostalgic storytelling and less so in a bare statement of fact.

One purely formal point causes more errors than anything else here. In the negative and the question, the d disappears: didn’t use to, Did you use to…? Writing didn’t used to is extremely common and is not accepted in careful English. And do not confuse this structure with be used to or get used to + -ing, which mean ‘be accustomed to’ and have nothing to do with past habits.

Typical situations

You need this for describing how life, work or a place has changed, telling somebody about your childhood, and contrasting the way things were with the way they are now.

  • Repeated past actions — used to or would, both fine.People used to stay in the same job for forty years.
  • Past states and situations — used to only — would is impossible here.There used to be a factory where the offices are now.
  • Something no longer true — the implied contrast with now.I used to hate meetings. Now I quite enjoy them.
  • Nostalgic storytelling — would, once the past frame is set, is the natural narrative choice.My grandfather would tell me the names of all the trees.
  • A single past habit repeated over years — would with a time marker.In those days children would learn everything by heart.
  • Contrasting then and now — often paired explicitly.Things aren’t like they used to be.

How it differs from similar structures

used to = actions and states · would = actions only. If you cannot picture somebody doing it, would is out.
used to + base verb = a past habit that has ended · be / get used to + -ing = being or becoming accustomed. I used to drive vs I’m used to driving.

How to build it

Affirmative: subject + used to + base verb  ·  subject + would + base verb
Negative: subject + didn’t use to + base verb  (no d after use)
Question: Did + subject + use to + base verb?
State: used to be / used to have + …  (never would be / would have)
AffirmativeI used to work nights. · We would meet every Friday.
NegativeI didn’t use to like it. · We wouldn’t talk about pay.
QuestionDid you use to work there? · Did people use to think the Earth was flat?
Short answersYes, I did. / No, we didn’t.
States — used to onlyThere used to be a canteen. · He used to have long hair.
With adverbsalways, often, never sit before would: He would always arrive early.

Spelling and word order

  • In the negative and the question the d disappears: didn’t use to, Did you use to…? Writing didn’t used to is very common but is not accepted in careful English.
  • Do not confuse used to + base verb (past habit) with be used to / get used to + -ing (be accustomed to something). They look alike and mean different things.

Saying it — contractions and stress

  • used to is pronounced /ˈjuːstə/ — with an s sound, not a z, and the two words run together.
  • would is normally reduced to ’d after a pronoun: he’d tell me. Learners often miss it entirely in listening.
  • ’d here is would, and the base verb after it proves it: he’d tell (would) versus he’d told (had).

Usage notes and exceptions

  • Would cannot describe a state. I would have long hair and There would be a factory are wrong. States take used to or the past simple.
  • Would normally needs the past time frame to be set already. Starting a story with I would walk to school is odd; When I was ten, I would walk to school is natural.
  • Used to has no present form. For a present habit, use the present simple: I walk to work, never I use to walk.
  • Be used to + -ing means ‘be accustomed to’: I’m used to working nights. Get used to + -ing means ‘become accustomed to’: I got used to working nights. Neither is about past habits.
  • The past simple with a frequency adverb is always a safe alternative: I often worked nights. Use it when you are unsure whether the situation is a state or an action.

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • I didn’t used to like my job. → I didn’t use to like my job.The d disappears after didn’t.
  • There would be a factory here. → There used to be a factory here.Would cannot express a state.
  • I use to walk to work every day now. → I walk to work every day.Used to has no present form.
  • I’m used to work nights. → I’m used to working nights.Be used to takes the -ing form.
  • Did you used to supervise a team? → Did you use to supervise a team?After did, the base form use.
  • He would be a director in those days. → He used to be a director in those days.Be is a state, so would is impossible.

More examples in context

  • past habitPeople used to stay with one employer for their whole working life.
  • past stateThere used to be a canteen where the open-plan office is now.
  • changeI didn’t use to mind the commute, but now it exhausts me.
  • narrativeIn those days managers would write everything down by hand.
  • repeated actionEvery Friday the whole floor would go out together.
  • questionDid you use to get sick pay in your last job?
  • contrastThings aren’t what they used to be — nobody has a fixed desk now.
  • state, negativeWe didn’t use to have flexible hours.
  • adverb positionShe would always arrive before anyone else.
  • distinguishingI used to work nights, so I’m used to working when everyone else is asleep.

A tip for remembering it

Run two checks. Check one: is it an action or a state? A state (be, have, know, live, like) can only take used to. Check two: is there a did in the sentence? If so, drop the d from used. Those two checks catch almost every error with this structure.

Before you practise — the key rules

  1. Used to + base verb = a past habit or state that is no longer true.
  2. Would + base verb = a repeated past action only, never a state.
  3. In negatives and questions the d disappears: didn’t use to, Did you use to…?
  4. Used to has no present form — use the present simple.
  5. Would needs a past time frame already established.
  6. Be / get used to + -ing is a different structure meaning ‘accustomed to’.

Stage 5 · Main input

The way we used to work

Forty-one years in one building, and what was gained and lost.

Before you read: working life has changed enormously in the last fifty years.

Which change do you think matters most?

Choose one. The text discusses all three — see which one it ends on.

The way we used to work

Fifty years ago, most people expected one employer, one office and one pension. Almost every part of that has gone.

AThere was a time when a young person would leave school, walk into a local firm and stay there. My grandfather worked for the same company for forty-one years. He used to say that changing jobs looked unreliable — that an employer would want to know why you had left. The average worker today changes employer roughly every four to five years, and nobody asks that question any more.

BSome occupations have disappeared entirely. Before alarm clocks were cheap, British factory towns employed knocker-uppers, who would walk the streets before dawn tapping on bedroom windows with a long stick until the sleeper appeared. Large offices had typing pools, where thirty or forty women would sit in rows typing what other people had written. Telegram boys, lift operators, lamplighters: none of these jobs was unskilled, and none of them exists now.

CThe working day was different too, and not always in the direction people imagine. Hours were long, but the boundaries were solid. When my grandfather left the building, he had left. There was no way for the office to reach him, and nobody expected it to. He used to describe his working conditions as hard but simple: you obeyed the rules, you followed the procedures, and in return the firm was supposed to look after you until you retired.

DWhat replaced it is more relaxed and much less certain. Dress codes have almost gone. Many people can work from home, choose their own hours, or take a temporary contract that suits a particular year of their life. But the promise on the other side of that arrangement has gone as well. Very few employers now offer anything that resembles a lifetime, and the person who used to be looked after is expected to manage their own training, their own pension and their own reputation.

EWhether this is progress depends on where you stand. People with skills that are in demand have never had more freedom: they can quit, negotiate, retrain or move country. People without them have inherited the insecurity without the freedom. The same change produced both outcomes, which is why arguments about modern work so often talk past each other.

FMy grandfather, who lived long enough to see the beginning of all this, was not nostalgic about it. He would point out that his forty-one years were not really a choice; there was nothing else, and leaving was frightening. “You had one life and one job,” he said, “and you hoped they suited each other.” What he valued was not the job. It was knowing, at twenty-five, roughly what the next forty years would look like — and that, more than any occupation, is what has actually disappeared.

Written for this course. Employment-tenure and occupational-change figures are drawn from published national labour statistics and occupational histories.
